value.overview: The Black-necked Stilt is a striking shorebird of shallow wetlands, recognized by its extremely long pink legs, slender straight bill, black-and-white plumage, and loud alarm calls. It lives in freshwater and saline environments across much of the Americas. In Costa Rica, it is associated mainly with lowland wetlands, coastal lagoons, estuaries, salt ponds, flooded fields, and lake margins. Some birds remain year-round, while others occur during migration or the nonbreeding season.
value.classification: The Black-necked Stilt belongs to the avocet and stilt family Recurvirostridae and the genus Himantopus. The mainland American form is treated as Himantopus mexicanus; related stilt populations are sometimes classified separately or as subspecies.
value.identification: Adults are slender, long-legged waders with a white breast and underparts, glossy black wings and back, and a black head and neck pattern. The long legs are usually bright pink to reddish, and the bill is thin, straight, and black. In flight, the black wings contrast strongly with the white body. Females may show a brownish cast on the back, while juveniles are duller and have less sharply defined dark markings. Its tall, elegant shape makes it difficult to confuse with most other Costa Rican shorebirds.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from the western and southern United States through Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and much of South America. In Costa Rica, it is recorded in both coastal and inland lowlands, including Guanacaste, the Pacific coastal plain, the Gulf of Nicoya region, and other suitable wetlands. It uses estuaries, mudflats, mangroves, shallow freshwater ponds, seasonally flooded fields, marshes, lake edges, and salt or shrimp ponds. It generally favors open areas with shallow water and exposed muddy or sparsely vegetated ground.
value.migrationStatus: Costa Rica has both resident and migratory Black-necked Stilts. Birds breeding farther north may pass through or winter in the country, while some local birds remain year-round; the species is listed in Costa Rica as both resident and migratory.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs in open wetlands such as marshes, wet savannas, shallow ponds, mudflats, flooded fields, and margins of coastal lagoons. The nest is a shallow scrape or small platform made from mud, sticks, shells, or other available debris, often on a slightly raised site surrounded by water or with a broad view. Both adults participate in incubation and defense. Usually four, sometimes fewer or more, buff-colored eggs are marked with dark spots. Chicks are precocial and leave the nest soon after hatching.
value.dietFeeding: Black-necked Stilts feed mainly in shallow water and on wet mud. Their prey includes aquatic and terrestrial insects, flies, beetles, crustaceans, brine shrimp, small mollusks, worms, tadpoles, and small fish. They pick prey from the surface, probe soft sediment, and sweep or peck with the bill while wading. Food choices vary with habitat: brine-related prey is important in saline wetlands, while insects, snails, small fish, and other aquatic animals are common in freshwater sites.
value.behavior: This species is active and conspicuous, often walking through shallow water with measured steps while constantly searching for prey. It is highly vocal, especially when nesting, and adults may aggressively chase hawks, gulls, mammals, or people that approach a colony. Threat displays include calling, flying directly at an intruder, and feigning injury to draw predators away from young. Black-necked Stilts may gather in loose groups outside the breeding season and frequently roost on small islands, bars, or exposed muddy margins.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered broadly stable, with regional increases and declines. Trends can differ substantially among wetland systems and geographic populations.
conservation.threats: Wetland drainage, conversion of shallow ponds and coastal flats, altered water levels, disturbance at nesting sites, pollution, and loss of wetland prey can reduce local numbers. In Costa Rica, protection and careful management of estuaries, mangroves, salt ponds, flooded fields, and freshwater wetlands are important for maintaining suitable habitat.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore shallow wetlands, coastal lagoons, estuaries, mangroves, and seasonally flooded fields. Maintain natural water regimes, limit pesticide and other pollutant runoff, and avoid disturbing nesting birds or entering colonies during the breeding season. Supporting wetland reserves and reporting sightings through established bird-monitoring programs can improve knowledge of Costa Rican populations.
